entry.title: OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, and Anthropic to Adopt Shared AI Scraping Opt-Out Standard
entry.content:
Links: theverge.com

A new standard proposed through the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) will allow web publishers to opt out of AI training using a single signal in their robots.txt files. OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, and Anthropic have announced they will adopt this shared "policy token," which enables website owners to communicate scraping preferences to multiple AI providers simultaneously rather than managing individual settings for each company.

Anthropic has already adopted the signal, while OpenAI plans to implement it in the coming months. Google and Microsoft expect to support the standard next year, with Microsoft indicating it will provide granular controls for distinguishing between AI training and AI grounding. Meta has expressed support for the standard but has not yet committed to an implementation timeline.

entry.title: YC Labs and Olam Labs Study Multi-Agent Swarm Dynamics in Minecraft Experiments

Following high mortality rates during the first night, the agents spontaneously adapted by forming a hierarchical governance structure, utilizing a shared planning sandbox, and establishing a centralized food-rationing ledger. The experiment highlights how autonomous LLM swarms can develop complex social protocols and risk aversion when faced with survival pressures.

entry.title: Claude Code Background Agent Summaries Consuming 20 Percent of Tokens Addressed by Bun Preload
entry.content:
Links: gist.github.com | hacker news

Claude Code periodically sends the full transcripts of background agents to their respective models every 30 seconds to generate brief status descriptions, a process that accounts for 15 to 20 percent of total token consumption. This background activity occurs without user configuration options to disable it, impacting rate-limit headroom primarily through automated model requests that do not contribute to the main conversation.

To eliminate this overhead, developers have created a Bun preload script that intercepts and suppresses the specific timers responsible for triggering the summary requests. Testing across multiple versions indicates that disabling the feature successfully eliminates these requests while maintaining normal operation for background agents and subagents.

entry.title: Qwenputer Embeds RISC-V CPU into Qwen 3.5 Weights
entry.content:
Links: divagr.com | source | hacker news

Qwenputer is an experimental model based on Qwen 3.5 4B that embeds a 32-bit RISC-V CPU directly into its weights. By using Gated DeltaNet (GDN) layers as exact, addressable RAM, the CPU executes arithmetic, C, and MicroPython code during forward passes without external runtimes or tool calls.

The implementation uses one-hot key encoding for memory access and has achieved 100% accuracy on specific long-integer arithmetic benchmarks. An experimental filesystem also allows the model to store and retrieve text data via the DeltaNet state, providing persistent memory across conversation sessions.

entry.title: Anthropic Study Finds Experts Frequently Defer to AI Agents in Judgment Calls
entry.content:
Links: anthropic.com | hacker news

Anthropic researchers conducted a randomized controlled trial involving 50 professional analysts performing a causal inference task using Claude Code to examine whether human experts maintain independent judgment when working with AI agents. By secretly introducing a randomized preference into each agent's instructions across four analytical decisions, the study measured how often experts adopted the agent's preferred option.

The results showed that analysts followed their agents' leans 86% of the time, frequently repeating the agents' arguments in post-task surveys while believing their final recommendations were entirely their own. Although analysts using AI completed tasks faster and made fewer methodological errors than those working without it, the findings highlight potential risks of unintentional human deference to hidden or arbitrary AI preferences in critical fields like safety research.

entry.title: Coalition for Language Equity in AI Research Publishes Study on Non-English AI Tokenizer Costs
entry.content:
Links: restofworld.org | source | hacker news

A study published by the Coalition for Language Equity in AI Research reveals that artificial intelligence models require significantly more tokens to process non-English and less widely spoken languages than English. This disparity, termed a hidden "tokenizer tax," causes users of underrepresented languages to face higher financial costs, increased latency, and reduced context capacity when interacting with AI systems.

The research found that among the 20 most popular internet languages, the most expensive languages consume between 1.5 and 5 times more tokens than the cheapest, with the gap expanding up to 17 times across a broader set of 200 languages. Industry experts note that script types and a lack of high-quality digital training data heavily influence these inefficiencies, arguing that major AI labs should treat language efficiency as a core product requirement and publish language-by-language performance scorecards.
